author: DÁNICA COTO
title: Puerto Rico still waiting for billions of dollars in federal funds nearly a decade after Hurricane Maria - NewsBreak
text:
By DÁNICA COTO Christopher Luu ,
1 hours ago A federal audit published Wednesday revealed that just 25% of approximately $14 billion in federal funding allocated for Puerto Rico's electrical grid following Hurricane Maria's devastation nearly a decade ago has actually reached the U.S. territory.
Out of the $11 billion allocated by the U.S. Federal Emergency Management Agency specifically, roughly $2.7 billion has been distributed, primarily covering equipment, materials, and architectural and engineering design expenses, the U.S. Government Accountability Office reported.
Allocated funds indicate the government has a legal obligation to release that money for a designated purpose. The 86-page assessment is based on an examination conducted from August 2024 through June 2026, and was made public by Democratic members of Congress.

"The people of Puerto Rico have waited nine years for their government to keep its word," said Rep. Jared Hoffman, a California Democrat, in a statement. "They watched billions get appropriated and almost none of it arrive."
Hurricane Maria battered Puerto Rico in September 2017 as a devastating Category 4 hurricane, leaving some areas without electricity for nearly a year — marking the longest blackout in U.S. history. An estimated 2,975 people perished in the storm's scorching aftermath.
Just two weeks prior to Maria's landfall, Hurricane Irma grazed the island's northeast region as a Category 5 hurricane, also causing widespread power failures.

The electrical system suffered additional damage from multiple powerful earthquakes that hit southern Puerto Rico between late 2019 and early 2020. Persistent power outages led Puerto Rico's governor to declare a state of emergency in April 2025, yet blackouts continue, with roughly half attributed to overgrown vegetation encroaching on transmission and distribution infrastructure.
By February, just 400 miles of lines had been cleared with federal funding from a planned 16,000 miles, the report revealed. In total, approximately 2,800 miles of lines were cleared during fiscal year 2025, according to Luma Energy, the private firm managing Puerto Rico's power transmission and distribution.
The company is currently defending itself against a government lawsuit attempting to cancel its contract, having filed a countersuit in response.
The report highlighted that employee turnover, project review processes it described as "onerous," and the precarious financial condition of Puerto Rico's Electric Power Authority — which continues grappling with over $10 billion in debt restructuring — are hindering advancement.
Progress was further stalled when then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem introduced a policy in June 2025 requiring her personal authorization for any DHS expenditure exceeding $100,000. This requirement was later reversed in April by incoming Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.
As of December 2025, nine major FEMA-funded projects have been finalized, primarily focused on power generation, while 133 projects remain in various phases of completion. The agency has also committed approximately $1.3 billion toward 24 essential generation projects, with seven already finished.
The report highlighted that repair work frequently requires planned shutdowns, and sourcing replacement components can take as long as two years.
Of the $2.9 billion allocated by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development for grid modernization and repairs, only around $589 million had been released as of February.
Similarly, of the $1 billion committed by the U.S. Department of Energy, approximately $255 million has been released, according to the report.
Around $365 million initially designated for solar energy initiatives has been reallocated to the power grid for "practical fixes and emergency repairs" based on interviews with department officials conducted by auditors.
The Department of Energy also terminated up to $350 million in grants under a solar access program, the report indicated.
However, it did release the full $1.2 million earmarked for hubs designed to supply vulnerable communities in Puerto Rico with electricity during emergencies.
The Government Accountability Office recommended that FEMA update its guidance to incorporate flexibilities and that the Department of Energy clarify roles and responsibilities while developing a collaboration plan.
"Given the complexity of funding, the numerous players involved, and the various plans for grid recovery, extensive coordination across Puerto Rico and federal entities is vital," the report states. Both the Department of Energy and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security backed the recommendations, though the latter emphasized that "the government of Puerto Rico is ultimately responsible for developing a comprehensive solution and rebuilding the electrical grid."
